CheriBSD's revocation sweeps capabilities to freed heap memory, so the stale pointer SHOULD be revoked and the probe fault -- but only if the sweep has run between the free and the access. The reduction frees and re-allocates immediately, the case least favourable to revocation, so a clean reading here would be about sweep TIMING rather than about the defect. It must be read in-guest before it is called either way.

title: a teardown helper frees the struct it is handed, and the caller freed it again
object: the k12_t file-state struct, one g_malloc from new_k12_file_data()
lifetime_ender: destroy_k12_file_data(file_data), whose last statement is g_free(fd)
shape: a callee that frees its argument, followed by the caller freeing it again
allocator_layer: the platform allocator itself: one direct g_malloc-family allocation, no wmem layer. GLib's g_malloc is malloc plus abort-on-failure.
fidelity: model consumer, real lifetime: the allocation, the free and the later access through the stale pointer are upstream's, quoted in PROVENANCE.md. The later access is the caller's own `g_free(file_data);` on the next line.
status: built 2026-10-08; native arms measured by runners/run-native.sh in the same commit. The platform arms are declared predictions.
live_proof: absent at the pin: `grep -c 'g_free(file_data);'` on v4.6.8:wiretap/k12.c is 0, while `destroy_k12_file_data(file_data);` appears 14 times. The fix is a REMOVAL, so zero occurrences of the removed line is the fix being present. A fix-reversal.
nested_why: the object came straight from g_malloc / g_new / g_new0 / g_strdup / getline -- which on the platform is malloc -- with no wmem allocator between it and the request. So under this inventory's axis, WHO ALLOCATED THE OBJECT, this row is NOT nested. Its sibling ../wmem-repros holds the nested ones.
distinguishing: the free is INVISIBLE at the call site: `destroy_k12_file_data` reads as 'destroy the contents', and only its last line frees the struct itself. That is why the fix deletes the caller's free rather than adding a null assignment, and why the same mistake appears at four separate error paths in one function.
